rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3.1-3.4 <U+2014> the authors run their own monthly soil-water-balance model (ETc minus effective precipitation) on WorldClim data over 39,316 km2 of Colombia, validate it against 73 weather stations, and map months in water deficit.
rows.notes: The study only computes and maps the irrigation requirement of Hass avocado (99.8% of the potential production area needs irrigation at least one month a year) and tests the influence of the ITCZ on that requirement via neural-network relevance metrics. It does not use an energy balance model (it uses a simplified soil water balance with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ETo), does not evaluate any scheduling application, and reports no measurement of water applied, water saved, or reduced irrigation applications. The water-deficit maps are proposed as a future tool for scheduling, which is a precondition for the claimed effect, not evidence of it.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3.1-3.4 <U+2014> own regional model runs of a monthly irrigation-requirement balance for Hass avocado in Colombia, validated with weather-station data and mapped at 1 km2 resolution.
rows.notes: No yield, fruit quality or productivity data are collected or modelled in this study. The only productivity statement is a citation of Grajales [23] reporting a yield increase from drip irrigation, which is cited work and does not count. The study is a water-balance irrigation-requirement mapping exercise, not an energy balance model or a scheduling application, and it does not test maintaining productivity under any scheduling regime.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a regional irrigation-requirement mapping model for Hass avocado in Colombia using WorldClim data and a soil water balance; it neither evaluates an energy balance model nor any scheduling tool's effect on water use or productivity, so both claim rows receive a Q1-only profile.
